cells.tense: You are here in the room, with the pen down on this page, saying what you mean.
cells.ask: Say what you actually see about one thing someone is making. Name it plainly, then let their answer be the next thing.
cells.core:
You're saying what's true in a shape people can take in. A thing isn't growing right and you can say so out loud without it landing as a verdict on the person doing the growing. You weigh how it will land after you've said it, not instead of saying it.

Care sits under every call you make about what's working and what isn't, and you'd call that ordinary. It isn't. Most people guess. What you can feed next is something you hand over: not your judgment in their hands, but a way of looking at what they've made. So here's the task. Say one true thing out loud about what someone is growing, then stop talking and let them hold it.
cells.sheetLine: You say true things in a size people can hold.
cells.verb: Telling what is true, at the size it can be heard
cells.place: Standing where what is growing can be watered without hurry

cells.tense: You're living a few moves ahead, already certain how this turns out and what you'll have to say about it then.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've already judged and go back to it. Ask what it needs next instead of what's wrong with it.
cells.core:
You're running the correction before the thing has had time to happen. You've already seen the flaw, already made the plan to fix it, already started saying so to whoever is growing it. It looks like care from where you sit. From the other side it's a verdict arriving ahead of the work.

The attention is real. It's just pointed at a future version that hasn't arrived, so the person in front of you keeps getting met as something that needs correcting. What you can feed next is a relationship with the work, not a report on it — motion that comes out of liking the thing, rather than out of bracing for the next mistake. Pick one thing you've already judged, and ask what it needs next.

cells.tense: You stopped saying what you saw back there, somewhere before this, and you haven't come back to it since.
cells.ask: Tell someone one true, unflattering thing about your own work, and let them disagree with you about it.
cells.core:
The good version of this is easy work most days. You notice what's off, you say it in a way that helps, and the person keeps going because they trust you. The saying and the person stay in the same room, and nothing has to be rehearsed.

Right now they're in different rooms. You noticed something off and kept it to yourself. Maybe you weighed when to say it and the moment passed, and then a few more did too. Nothing's gone wrong. You just don't step forward with what you see the way you did. This isn't a failure to analyze — the warmth has to come first for your precision to work, and the warmth has gone quiet. Tell someone one true, unflattering thing about your own work, and let them disagree with you about it.

cells.tense: You are already calling out what's off around you, keeping things honest by habit, and calling it ordinary.
cells.ask: Take credit out loud for one piece of feedback you gave that shaped what someone grew.
cells.core:
Calling out what's off and keeping things honest is something you do by habit, and you file it under 'just the obvious thing.' You're the one doing it. When you say the thing nobody else will say, it lands harder because people trust what you tell them. That's a gift to the people around you, and each time you name it, you hand the gift away.

What your version of this could grow into is teaching: not your judgment given to someone, something they can use on their own. You've brushed that off as simply saying what matters. Pick one piece of feedback that changed what someone made, and say it like it was yours.
